paper_title: Different Tasks, Different Timesteps: Temporal Task-Aware Quantization for Diffusion Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) introduce unique quantization challenges due to their iterative denoising process. In this work, we reveal that quantization sensitivity is both taskand time-dependent, with different downstream tasks exhibiting distinct precision requirements across denoising steps. We further show that these patterns can be predicted without groundtruth labels or task-specific evaluation metrics. Building on these findings, we introduce T 2Quant, a task and time-aware mixedprecision quantization framework that uses a label-free sensitivity signal to optimally allocate activation precision across denoising steps under a fixed bit-width budget. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that T 2Quant consistently improves the average accuracy of existing quantization methods, achieving gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under the same budget.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have emerged as compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, generating text through iterative denoising with bidirectional context and parallel token prediction (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025). However, iterative denoising requires repeated model evaluations, making efficient inference increasingly important. Quantization is widely adopted technique for reducing the memory footprint and computational cost of large language models. However, methods developed for AR models may not directly transfer to DLMs due to their distinct step-wise decoding dynamics. Recent studies have identified DLMspecific quantization challenges, including activation outliers, timestep-dependent distributions, and accumulated quantization errors (Lin et al., 2026; Xu and Yang, 2025; Yan et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). While these methods improve quantization 1 Figure 1: Task-dependent temporal sensitivity to activation quantization. Each curve shows, per eight-step denoising window, the KL divergence DKL(pfp pq) summed over the positions committed in that window that the tasks scoring function reads. robustness, they generally maintain fixed activation precision throughout the denoising process. Meanwhile, temporal mixed-precision allocation has been explored in image diffusion models (Lewandowski et al., 2026), and recent studies on DLMs have highlighted how step-wise dynamics, intermediate predictions, and token commitment decisions influence generation behavior (Zhang et al., 2026b; Rahimi et al., 2026; Shlomi et al., 2026). Nevertheless, how quantization sensitivity varies jointly across downstream tasks and denoising steps in DLMs, and how these variations can guide effective mixed-precision allocation, remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we systematically investigate the sensitivity of DLMs to activation quantization across different tasks and denoising steps. Our analysis reveals that precision importance is both task-dependent and time-dependent (Figure 1): different tasks exhibit distinct temporal sensitivity patterns, with some benefiting more from higher precision during early denoising steps and others exhibiting greater sensitivity at intermediate stages. Figure 2: T2Quant overview. (1) few unlabeled prompts per task are profiled with the full-precision and quantized models. (2) Divergence influence gives the predicted gain of upscaling each denoising window. (3) An exact dynamic program selects the windows to upscale under the bit budget. (4) The result is task-specific schedule at the same average precision as uniform Atarget. Furthermore, we find that the benefit of additional precision can be predicted without ground-truth labels or downstream metric evaluations. Specifically, we develop label-free sensitivity signal that combines quantization-induced divergence with the downstream influence of each denoising stage, enabling the identification of task-specific precision requirements using only unlabeled calibration prompts. Building on these findings, we introduce T2Quant (Task and Time-Aware Quantization), mixed-precision framework that allocates activation precision across denoising steps according to task-specific sensitivity patterns (Figure 2). T2Quant leverages the proposed sensitivity signal to determine an optimal precision schedule under fixed average bit-width budget through budgetconstrained dynamic programming. Our framework is complementary to existing post-training quantization methods and can be integrated with different quantization approaches without modifying their underlying quantizers. Extensive experiments across three DLMs and six benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in average accuracy under fixed budget, outperforming the strongest evaluated quantized baselines by up to 6.7 percentage points. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Task and time-dependent precision sensitivity. We reveal distinct temporal precision sensitivity patterns across downstream tasks in DLMs. Label-free sensitivity prediction. We predict precision importance using internal model signals, without ground-truth labels or taskspecific evaluation metrics. Task and time-aware mixed-precision quantization. We introduce T2Quant, which optimally allocates activation precision under fixed bit budget and improves existing quantization methods.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: DLM Quantization. DLMs such as LLaDA and Dream generate text by iterative masked denoising with bidirectional context rather than left-to-right decoding (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025), which raises quantization challenges absent from autoregressive LLMs. DLLMQuant introduces diffusionaware calibration and quantization (Xu and Yang, 2025); STaR-Quant uses state-guided transformations and temporal compensation (Yan et al., 2026); FAIR-Calib targets fragile denoising states (Huang et al., 2026); and Quant-dLLM explores sensitivitybased mixed precision (Zhang et al., 2026a). These methods show that diffusion state and temporal error propagation matter, yet all keep fixed activation bit-width across the denoising trajectory. We instead treat activation precision as resource allocated over denoising steps under fixed average bit budget. Task-Aware Quantization. Task-Aware Quantization (TAQ) estimates layer importance from small task-specific calibration set and assigns higher weight precision to task-relevant layers under fixed bit budget (LeVi et al., 2026), and Task-Circuit Quantization (TaCQ) preserves identified from task-relevant weight circuits, 2 quantization-induced weight changes and gradientbased impact estimates, at higher precision (Xiao et al., 2025). Both show that the best allocation of quantization budget depends on the task, but they allocate precision spatially, across layers or weights of autoregressive LLMs. In contrast, T2Quant explores temporal task dependence, allocating activation precision across denoising steps according to task-specific sensitivity. Temporal Precision Scheduling. Temporal variation is recognized factor in image diffusion quantization: Q-Diffusion uses timestep-aware calibration for shifting activation distributions, and correction methods compensate for errors accumulated across denoising steps (Li et al., 2023). Most closely related, TMPDiff assigns different precisions to different denoising timesteps in image diffusion models, modeling the final latent deviation as an approximately additive sum of pertimestep errors and searching over schedules built from single-timestep sensitivities (Lewandowski et al., 2026). DLMs differ qualitatively: generation consists of discrete, often irreversible token commitments, latent reconstruction error does not directly reflect downstream correctness, and timesteps importance depends on which task-relevant tokens it commits. Rather than single global schedule, T2Quant allocates activation precision per task, linking where quantization disrupts task-relevant generation to where additional precision should be spent.

sections.title: Across Diffusion Steps
sections.content: The iterative generation process of DLMs raises fundamental question for quantization: when does numerical precision matter most? Each denoising step operates on different partially generated state, with token commitments potentially influencing subsequent predictions (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025). Consequently, the impact of quantization may depend not only on the denoising step but also on the downstream task. Understanding these variations, and whether they can be predicted, motivates three research questions: RQ1: Where does quantization sensitivity occur in time? RQ2: Is temporal sensitivity task-dependent? RQ3: Can we predict where additional precision is most valuable? We address RQ1 and RQ2 through temporal divergence analysis (Section 3.1), and RQ3 through label-free precision-allocation proxy (Section 3.2). Experimental setup. We evaluate LLaDA-8BInstruct (Nie et al., 2025) on three tasks with distinct output structures: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and MMLUPro (Wang et al., 2024). We use 512-token generations over 128 denoising steps with single 512-token block, partitioning the trajectory into 16 non-overlapping windows of eight steps. We use the standard low-confidence remasking sampler of Nie et al. (2025) with temperature 0 and no classifier-free guidance. The quantized model uses QuaRot-style rotations (Ashkboos et al., 2024), 4bit GPTQ weights (Frantar et al., 2023), and dynamic per-token 4-bit activations. The target precision is Atarget = 4 bits and the upscaled precision is Aup = 8 bits. Further details are given in Appendix E. 3.1 Temporal Sensitivity Diagnostic Temporal sensitivity. Figure 1 shows that quantization sensitivity is highly non-uniform across the denoising trajectory. uniform distribution would assign each of the 16 eight-step windows Instead, 6.25% of the task-relevant divergence. on GSM8K the first window alone carries 27% (4.4 uniform) and the first quarter 55%, while on HumanEval five mid-trajectory windows (steps 3271) carry 52%. Even MMLU-Pro, the most evenly spread task, varies by nearly 2 between its most and least sensitive windows. This concentration suggests that activation precision need not be allocated uniformly over time and motivates selectively increasing precision at the most sensitive stages, as explored for image diffusion models (Lewandowski et al., 2026). Key Takeaway Quantization sensitivity varies across denoising steps. Task-dependent sensitivity. The location and spread of these sensitive regions vary substantially across tasks. GSM8K is strongly front-loaded, with its peak in the first 8 denoising steps and rapid decay thereafter. MMLU-Pro is also early, but broad: its first four windows (steps 031) are all 3 within 10% of its peak, after which sensitivity declines gradually. In contrast, HumanEval is insensitive early and exhibits broad mid-trajectory peak, roughly around steps 4063. Thus, single task-independent temporal precision schedule is unlikely to suit all tasks. Whether these sensitivity profiles can predict where additional precision actually improves downstream performance is examined in Section 3.2. Key Takeaway Sensitivity patterns differ across tasks, challenging fixed temporal precision schedules. 3.2 Label-Free Signal for Precision Allocation We now address RQ3: identifying, without downstream labels, which denoising windows benefit most from additional activation precision. Splits, sampler, quantization setup, baseline implementations and statistical tests are given in Appendix E.2. 5.2 Main Results Table 1 reports W4A4 accuracy across three DLMs and six benchmarks, comparing DLLMQuant, FAIR-Calib, and STaR-Quant with and without T2Quant. All configurations use 4-bit weights and the same average activation precision of 4.00 bits, ensuring fair comparison under identical bit budgets. Consistent improvements across methods and models. T2Quant improves average accuracy for all nine baseline/model combinations, with gains of up to 6.7 points on Dream, 3.4 on LLaDA-1.5, and 3.5 on LLaDA-8B-Instruct. Overall, 42 of 54 benchmark-level comparisons improve, with GSM8K and ARC-Challenge improving in every combination. Best quantized accuracy across all models. T2Quant achieves the two highest quantized averages on every model, outperforming the strongest standalone baselines by 3.55, 1.13, and 1.40 points on Dream, LLaDA-1.5, and LLaDA-8B-Instruct, respectively. The best configurations approach FP16 accuracy, with gaps of only 2.0, 2.5, and 1.6 points. Substantial recovery from quantization degradation. The largest gains occur on Dream, where GSM8K accuracy rises from 35.6 to 53.5 with DLLMQuant and from 46.1 to 58.8 with STaRQuant. On GSM8K, improvements also reach 9.6 points on LLaDA-1.5 and 10.4 on LLaDA-8BInstruct. On several benchmarks, T2Quant even matches or exceeds FP16 accuracy. Precision allocation matters. Building on this observation, we introduced T2Quant, taskand time-aware mixedprecision framework that predicts precision importance using unlabeled calibration prompts and allocates activation precision under fixed bit-width budget. Across three DLMs and six benchmarks, T2Quant consistently improves average accuracy when integrated with existing quantization methods, with gains of up to 6.7 percentage points under W4A4. These results highlight the importance of considering both task requirements and temporal generation dynamics when quantizing DLMs. By improving accuracy under fixed precision budgets, T2Quant offers promising direction for making DLM deployment more computationally efficient and accessible, potentially reducing memory and energy requirements. Its compatibility with existing quantization methods may further facilitate practical adoption. However, quantization can also alter model behavior beyond benchmark accuracy, including safety-related responses (Hong et al., 2024; Egashira et al., 2024). Future work should therefore examine the effects of taskand time-aware precision allocation on safety, robustness, and real-world inference efficiency. original baselines on Dream. In contrast, T2Quant achieves the best quantized average on every model, highlighting the importance of allocating precision to the appropriate denoising steps. 5.3 Ablation Study Figure 4 evaluates three aspects of T2Quant on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and GSM8K under W4A4 (uniform W4A4: 44.1, T2Quant: 49.4, FP16: 52.9). (a) Calibration size: Just 16 prompts recover roughly 75% of the full gain, with stable schedules consistently prioritizing early denoising steps. (b) Tokens per step: The schedule transfers from 4 to 2 tokens per step, maintaining an approximately 5point improvement, while gains vanish at 8 tokens per step as overall accuracy deteriorates. (c) Activation budget: T2Quant achieves 48.4% accuracy with only 3.75 average bits, outperforming uniform W4A4 (44.1%) despite using fewer bits. Moreover, T2Quant consistently outperforms random schedules at the same bit budget, while increasing precision beyond 4 bits provides negligible additional benefit. These results demonstrate that effective precision allocation matters more than simply increasing the bit budget. Further ablations, including window size, precision levels, the set of activation widths  (Table 2)  additional quantization budgets, and calibration signals, are provided in Appendix B.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Although T2Quant demonstrates strong results across three DLMs, six benchmarks, and three further evaluation of quantization methods, deployment-related aspects, including hardware efficiency (inference speed and energy consumption) and potential impacts on model safety, remains for future work.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: We used LLMs during manuscript preparation mainly as writing assistants, for grammar checking and for improving the clarity and naturalness of the text. All LLM-generated suggestions were manually reviewed and edited by the authors. LLMs did not play any important role in developing the core methods, experiments, analysis, or conclusions of this research.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: This work aims to improve the efficiency and accessibility of diffusion language models through quantization. While quantization may affect model safety and robustness, investigating these effects is left for future work.

sections.title: Appendix Overview
sections.content: This appendix provides supplementary analyses, additional experimental results, ablation studies, theoretical proofs, and implementation details that complement the main paper. It is organized as follows: Section presents further analyses and supplementary experimental results. Section provides additional ablation studies to further examine the proposed method. Section contains the theoretical proofs supporting the claims made in the main paper. Section provides detailed algorithms and pseudocode for the proposed method. Section details the experimental setup, implementation details, and evaluation protocols.

Bottom: correlation with held-out accuracy gains. HumanEval: damage rises to broad peak A.1 Temporal Sensitivity Diagnostic over steps 4064. We repeat the label-free diagnostic of Section 3 on two further masked-diffusion LMs: LLaDA1.5 (Zhu et al., 2026) and Dream-v0-Instruct7B (Ye et al., 2025). Generation: 512 tokens, 128 denoising steps in single block, greedy decoding. Quantization: the same W4A4 recipe (rotation, GPTQ W4, per-token A4 with clip 0.7) and calibration data. Tasks: the same subsets, prompts and scorers. Each model is quantized with single rotation seed. LLaDA-1.5. LLaDA-1.5 is LLaDA-8B-Instruct further trained with variance-reduced preference optimization (Zhu et al., 2026). Its architecture, tokenizer, sampler and EOS rules are unchanged. Figure 6 shows the resulting profiles, which closely match those of LLaDA-8B-Instruct (Figure 1). The Pearson correlation between the two models per-window profiles is 0.99 (GSM8K), 0.98 (HumanEval) and 0.92 (MMLU-Pro). GSM8K: damage peaks in the first window and decays. MMLU-Pro: damage forms broad early plateau, peaks at steps 1623 and rises again in the last window. LLaDA-1.5 is fine-tuned LLaDA-8B, so this result shows that the temporal profile survives preference alignment. It does not test other architectures; Dream addresses that below. Dream-v0-Instruct-7B. Dream uses its own sampler (Ye et al., 2025), which commits the lowest-entropy masked positions first. Everything else follows the shared setup; only the handling of the end-of-sequence (EOS) token differs. At the first denoising steps Dream predicts EOS at almost every masked position, so the EOS rule matters more than for LLaDA: No EOS rule (Dreams default): padding is committed first, and the answer is squeezed into the last few steps. LLaDAs rules: the few non-EOS positions are forced in first regardless of their confidence. Our choice: the confidence of positions predicting EOS or end-of-turn is lowered by 12 Figure 6: Label-free diagnostic for LLaDA-1.5 under W4A4, computed as in Figure 1: score-relevant KL per 8-step window, normalized to each tasks peak, with 95% problem-bootstrap bands. Figure 7: Label-free diagnostic for Dream-v0-Instruct7B under W4A4, computed as in Figure 1: scorerelevant KL per 8-step window, normalized to each tasks peak, with 95% problem-bootstrap bands. α = 1 nat, on all tasks. We chose α, and entropy over top-2-margin ordering, among six variants by full-precision accuracy on the first 20 problems of each task. The criterion was fixed before any damage profile was computed. The profiles in Figure 7 remain task-dependent, but the tasks peak at different points in denoising than on LLaDA. GSM8K: Dream answers directly under the shared answer-only few-shot prompt (about six tokens), so the damage concentrates in the first window, with small rise in the last one. HumanEval: damage stays low until step 64, then rises to peak at steps 96104, late rather than mid-trajectory as on LLaDA. MMLU-Pro: after first-window spike (most W4A4 responses state the answer first), damage ramps up steadily to the end.

Implementation Details
sections.content: Algorithms 1 and 2 describe the calibration and allocation stages of T2Quant. Following Section 3.2, calibration combines quantization divergence at all committed positions with downstream influence. The candidate precisions and resource costs remain symbolic; their experimental values are given in Appendix E. For each calibration prompt i, denoising step t, and activation precision b, define the committedposition divergence δi,t(b) = (cid:88) (cid:16) DKL i,t,jp(b) pfp i,t,j (cid:17) . jCi,t Conventions. Wi,k denotes the steps assigned to normalized window for prompt i, and equals Wk when all prompts use the same step count. The reference trajectory and all quantized replays use identical saved input states, as in Section 4.2. We assume Zk > 0 for every window. If no masked positions remain after window, its downstream influence is zero by Eq. (2). No ground-truth labels, task-specific evaluation metrics, or score-relevant position sets are used. The dynamic program requires O(KC0B) time and O(KC0) memory, where C0 is expressed in common integer cost unit. Its optimality guarantee applies to the additive surrogate of Eq. (5), not to downstream task accuracy. Rational costs can be converted into integer costs using common exact scaling. E.1 Model, Sampler, and Quantization Unless stated otherwise, all experiments use LLaDA-8B-Instruct with 512-token generations over 128 denoising steps in single 512-token block, so four positions are committed at each step. We use the standard low-confidence remasking sampler (Nie et al., 2025) with temperature 0 and no classifier-free guidance, so decoding is deterministic. End-of-sequence handling follows the official LLaDA evaluation settings for each benchmark. Rotations follow QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024): the residual stream is rotated by random Hadamard matrix, and online Hadamard transforms are applied before the attention output and MLP down projections. Weights of the transformer linear layers are quantized to 4 bits with GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) (per output channel, asymmetric, MSE-optimal clipping, act-order), calibrated on 128 WikiText (Merity et al., 2016) sequences of 512 tokens with random masking. The embeddings and language-model head remain in high precision. Activations are quantized dynamically per token, with clipping ratio of 0.7, at the inputs to the QKV projection, the attention output projection, the MLP up/gate projections, and the MLP down projection. Attention scores and softmax remain unquantized. We refer to the configuration with 4-bit weights and 4-bit activations as W4A4. The reference model uses BF16 computation, denoted fp16 throughout for consistency. For each benchmark the problems are drawn once from the original evaluation set and split into calibration pool and held-out evaluation pool; the calibration pool is the only data any calibrated method (the baselines and T2Quant) sees, and the heldout pool is the same for every row, so all comparisons in the paper are paired by problem. Every row uses the models upstream sampler unchanged: 4 tokens are unmasked per step with low-confidence remasking, at temperature 0, with the output lengths of Table 5. Rows therefore differ only in the quantization applied to the network. Quantization setup. Quantization is simulated (the quantized integer values are used in bf16 arithmetic), the standard protocol for post-training quantization studies (Ashkboos et al., 2024; Frantar et al., 2023). Weights are quantized to 4 bits per channel with GPTQ after Hadamard rotation of the hidden dimension (QuaRot-style, including the online rotation of the attention-output input). Activations, the inputs of all linear layers, are quantized dynamically per token; for widths below 8 bits the per-token range is clipped to 70% of its maximum. This rotated, GPTQ-quantized W4 model with pertoken A4 activations is the shared base of every quantized row except RTN, which uses round-tonearest 4-bit per-channel weights and per-token A4 activations without rotation or GPTQ. T2Quant keeps the base and varies only the activation width along the denoising trajectory: the trajectory is divided into 16 windows, each window uses one of {3, 4, 6, 8} bits, and the allocation is chosen on the calibration pool under an exact average of 4.00 bits (the method section gives the allocation). The random schedule assigns window widths at random under the same 4.00-bit average; one fixed draw (seed 0) is used for every model and benchmark. Baselines.
